The equation is **false** in general. Here is a counterexample.

---

**Claim:** The equation
$$P\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}\bar{X}_n=\mu\right)=\lim_{n\to\infty}P\left(\bar{X}_n=\mu\right)$$
does not hold in general for i.i.d. sequences with mean $\mu$.

**Counterexample.** Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be i.i.d. $N(\mu,1)$ random variables (normal with mean $\mu$ and variance $1$). Then $E[X_i]=\mu$, so the hypotheses are satisfied.

**Left-hand side.** Since the $X_i$ are i.i.d. with $E[|X_i|]<\infty$ and $E[X_i]=\mu$, the **Strong Law of Large Numbers** gives
$$\bar{X}_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} \mu,$$
that is,
$$P\!\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}\bar{X}_n = \mu\right) = 1.$$

**Right-hand side.** Since $\bar{X}_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ is a linear combination of independent normal random variables, it is itself normal:
$$\bar{X}_n \sim N\!\left(\mu,\;\frac{1}{n}\right).$$
This is a **continuous** distribution, so for every $n$,
$$P\!\left(\bar{X}_n = \mu\right) = 0.$$
Therefore
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}P\!\left(\bar{X}_n = \mu\right) = \lim_{n\to\infty} 0 = 0.$$

**Conclusion.** The left-hand side equals $1$ while the right-hand side equals $0$:
$$P\!\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}\bar{X}_n=\mu\right) = 1 \neq 0 = \lim_{n\to\infty}P\!\left(\bar{X}_n=\mu\right).$$
Hence the equation is **false**. $\blacksquare$

**Remark on why the interchange fails.** The left-hand side is the probability of the *limit event* $\{\omega : \bar{X}_n(\omega)\to\mu\}$, which the SLLN guarantees has probability $1$. The right-hand side is the limit of *point probabilities* $P(\bar{X}_n = \mu)$, each of which concerns the measure of the single point $\{\mu\}$ under the law of $\bar{X}_n$. For continuous distributions every singleton has measure zero, so each term on the right is $0$ regardless of $n$. The two operations—taking the probability of a limit event versus taking the limit of point-probabilities—are fundamentally different: almost-sure convergence describes behavior of *entire sample paths*, while $P(\bar{X}_n=\mu)$ captures only the instantaneous mass at one point. There is no general theorem permitting the interchange of $P$ and $\lim$ in this point-equality form, and the counterexample above shows the interchange is invalid.
